distraction.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F04"]},{"text":"Texting and the law.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F04"]}],"narration":{"text":"Welcome to the chapter on distracted driving and electronic communication devices. This first lesson explains why driving needs your full attention, what the guide means by a distraction, and the long list of everyday activities that count as distractions, including some that may surprise you. You will also learn why texting is singled out as by far the riskiest distraction, and what Missouri law says about texting while operating a vehicle. Later lessons cover passengers and pets, controls and devices, and the details of Missouri's electronic communication device law.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F04"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Full attention","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Constant coordination of mind and body.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},{"text":"A distraction keeps you from driving safely.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},{"text":"It puts everyone at risk.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Safe driving needs your full attention, because it involves constant and complex coordination between your mind and your body. You are watching the road, judging speed and distance, and moving your hands and feet, all at the same time. A distraction is anything that keeps you from operating the car safely, and every distraction puts drivers, passengers and bystanders at risk. So a distraction is not only a risk to you; the people in your car, other drivers and people walking or riding nearby all share that risk. The guide's list of distractions includes texting, phone use, eating and drinking, talking to passengers, adjusting audio players, grooming, reading maps, watching videos, browsing the Internet and using navigation.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":47,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"The guide's list","fact_ids":["sec17-F03","sec17-R11"]},"lines":[{"text":"Texting, phone use, eating and drinking.","fact_ids":["sec17-F03","sec17-R11"]},{"text":"Talking to passengers, grooming, audio.","fact_ids":["sec17-F03","sec17-R11"]},{"text":"Maps, videos, the Internet, navigation.","fact_ids":["sec17-F03","sec17-R11"]}],"narration":{"text":"The guide's list of distractions includes texting, phone use, eating and drinking, talking to passengers, adjusting audio players, grooming, reading maps, watching videos, browsing the Internet and using navigation. Some of these feel harmless, such as eating a snack or chatting with a friend, but each one takes part of your attention away from driving. Talking with passengers appears on the list alongside eating, grooming and reading. The more of these activities you combine, the less attention is left for the road and the people on it.","fact_ids":["sec17-F03","sec17-R11"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":35,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Why texting is worst","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Takes your eyes off the road.","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},{"text":"Takes your hands off the wheel.","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},{"text":"Takes your mind off driving.","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Texting takes your eyes, your hands and your mind off driving at once, which makes it by far the riskiest distraction. Reading a message pulls your eyes down, typing pulls your hands off the wheel, and thinking about what to write pulls your mind away from the traffic around you. Other distractions may take one of these at a time, but texting takes all three. Missouri law forbids anyone to read, write or send a text or other electronic message while operating a vehicle, so texting while driving is illegal as well as dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Passengers count too","fact_ids":["sec17-R11","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},"lines":[{"text":"Talking with passengers is on the list.","fact_ids":["sec17-R11","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},{"text":"Not only phones distract.","fact_ids":["sec17-R11","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers think of distraction as a phone problem only. The guide's list is much wider. Talking with passengers appears on the guide's list of distractions, alongside eating, grooming and reading. That does not mean you can never talk in the car, but it does mean conversation competes for the attention driving needs. A distraction is anything that keeps you from operating the car safely. On a test, if a question asks whether talking with passengers or eating can be a distraction, the answer is yes. The guide's list of distractions includes texting, phone use, eating and drinking, talking to passengers, adjusting audio players, grooming, reading maps, watching videos, browsing the Internet and using navigation.","fact_ids":["sec17-R11","sec17-F02","sec17-F03"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the texting rule","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Why is texting the riskiest?","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},{"text":"What does the law say?","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: why does the guide call texting by far the riskiest distraction, and what does Missouri law say about it? Work it out before reading on. Texting takes your eyes, your hands and your mind off driving at once, which is why it is by far the riskiest distraction. Missouri law forbids anyone to read, write or send a text or other electronic message while operating a vehicle. So texting is not just unsafe; it is illegal for every driver, whatever their age or experience, whenever they are operating a vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u01-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Distraction recap","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03","sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"lines":[{"text":"Full attention always.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03","sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},{"text":"Texting: eyes, hands, mind.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03","sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close: safe driving needs your full attention, because it involves constant and complex coordination between your mind and your body. The guide lists texting, phone use, eating and drinking, talking to passengers, adjusting audio, grooming, reading maps, watching videos, browsing the Internet and using navigation. Texting takes your eyes, hands and mind at once, and Missouri law forbids it while operating a vehicle.","fact_ids":["sec17-F01","sec17-F02","sec17-F03","sec17-F04","sec17-F05"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":34,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"}]},{"unit_id":"sec17-u02","module_id":"sec17-m02","objective_ids":["sec17-u02"],"title":{"text":"Passengers and pets","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08"]},"why_how":[{"text":"The people and animals riding with you can pull your attention away from the road.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06"]},{"text":"Simple choices, such as pulling over or securing a pet, remove those distractions.","fact_ids":["sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]}],"worked_example":{"scenario":{"text":"Rosa's dog keeps climbing toward her lap while she drives.","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10"]},"reasoning":{"text":"A loose pet in a moving vehicle can be very dangerous, and a pet should never sit on your lap.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},"result":{"text":"Rosa pulls over and secures the dog in a pet harness before driving on.","fact_ids":["sec17-F09"]}},"misconception":{"claim":{"text":"Common mistake: thinking it is fine to reach back and handle children while driving.","fact_ids":["sec17-F07"]},"correction":{"text":"If your children need attention, pull over to a safe place instead of handling them while driving.","fact_ids":["sec17-F07"]}},"memory_support":{"text":"Kids need you? Pull over. Pets? Crate them.","fact_ids":["sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"How should a pet travel in your car while you drive?","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10"]},"answer":{"text":"Secured in a carrier, portable kennel or pet harness, and never on your lap.","fact_ids":["sec17-F09"]},"rationale":{"text":"A loose pet in a moving vehicle can be very dangerous, so the pet is secured before the trip.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Who rides with you","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Children.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]},{"text":"Friends.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]},{"text":"Pets.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the passengers who can distract you: children, friends and pets. Each of them can become a dangerous distraction while you drive. You will learn what to do when your children need attention, what to teach young children about driving, how a car full of friends can pull your focus away, why upsetting conversations should wait, why a loose pet is dangerous, and how a pet should travel in your car. The common thread is that driving comes first, and the needs of passengers are handled in a safe place, not on the move.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":38,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Children","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull over to tend to children.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08"]},{"text":"Teach that driving needs focus.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08"]}],"narration":{"text":"Children, friends and pets can each become a dangerous distraction while you drive. If your children need attention, pull over to a safe place instead of handling them while driving. Reaching into the back seat or turning around takes your eyes, your hands and your attention off the road at once. The guide also suggests teaching young children that driving is an important job that needs your concentration when you are behind the wheel. Children who understand this are more likely to wait, which makes every trip calmer and safer for everyone.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Friends and conversations","fact_ids":["sec17-R09","sec17-F08"]},"lines":[{"text":"Loud talk, music arguments, horseplay.","fact_ids":["sec17-R09","sec17-F08"]},{"text":"Save arguments for a safe place.","fact_ids":["sec17-R09","sec17-F08"]}],"narration":{"text":"A car full of friends can distract you with loud talk, arguments over music, or horseplay. Each of these pulls your attention away from the road, and they often happen together. The guide also says to save arguments and upsetting conversations for a safe place, not for while you are driving. Strong emotions take up attention just as surely as a phone does. If a conversation becomes heated, it can wait until you have parked. Setting expectations with your friends before you start the trip helps keep the ride focused on safe driving.","fact_ids":["sec17-R09","sec17-F08"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":37,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s4","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Pets belong secured","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"A loose pet is very dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},{"text":"Use a carrier, kennel or harness.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},{"text":"Never on your lap.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers let a small pet ride loose or even on their lap, thinking it is calmer that way. The guide says a loose pet in a moving vehicle can be very dangerous. Secure a pet in a carrier, a portable kennel or a pet harness while driving, and never let it sit on your lap. A pet on your lap can block the wheel, the pedals or your view, and a loose pet can move suddenly at the worst moment. On a test, the safe answer always secures the pet before the trip. A loose pet in a moving vehicle can be very dangerous.","fact_ids":["sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s5","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the pet rule","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10","sec17-F07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dog in the car.","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10","sec17-F07"]},{"text":"How should it ride?","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10","sec17-F07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: you are taking your dog to the vet. How should the dog ride in your car while you drive? Work it out before reading on. Secure the dog in a carrier, a portable kennel or a pet harness, and never let it sit on your lap. A loose pet in a moving vehicle can be very dangerous, because it can move suddenly, block your view or get in the way of the controls. If the dog gets loose during the trip, pull over to a safe place to secure it again instead of reaching for it while driving. If your children need attention, pull over to a safe place instead of handling them while driving.","fact_ids":["sec17-F09","sec17-R10","sec17-F07"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u02-s6","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Passengers recap","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08","sec17-R09","sec17-F08","sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},"lines":[{"text":"Pull over for children.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08","sec17-R09","sec17-F08","sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]},{"text":"Arguments wait; pets secured.","fact_ids":["sec17-F06","sec17-F07","sec17-R08","sec17-R09","sec17-F08","sec17-R10","sec17-F09"]}],"narration":{"text":"To close: children, friends and pets can each become a dangerous distraction while you drive. If your children need attention, pull over to a safe place, and teach young children that driving is an important job that needs your concentration. A car full of friends can distract you with loud talk, arguments over music or horseplay, so save arguments and upsetting conversations for a safe place. adjust at stops.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14"]},"self_check":{"prompt":{"text":"When should you set your mirrors, seat, radio and climate controls?","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14"]},"answer":{"text":"Before you start to drive.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11"]},"rationale":{"text":"Set them before you go, and if something needs changing later, use a normal stop or ask a passenger.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14"]}},"slides":[{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s1","kind":"opening","title":{"text":"Controls and devices","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F15"]},"lines":[{"text":"Dials and screens.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F15"]},{"text":"Setting up before you go.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F15"]},{"text":"Eyes on the road.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F15"]}],"narration":{"text":"This lesson covers the distractions built into the car and the devices you carry, and the ones you see out the window. You will learn why working in-vehicle controls is risky, what to set before you start to drive, when to check email and voicemail, how a phone auto-reply can help, and how to handle adjustments during a trip. You will also learn why staring at roadside scenes, such as a crash or a billboard, counts as a distraction, and what the guide asks you to do instead so that you reach your destination safely. Entering a destination, scanning radio stations or changing climate settings can lead to a crash or near-crash, and Internet and email access add more risk.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F15"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":48,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s2","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Turning dials turns your head","fact_ids":["sec17-R12","sec17-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Entering destinations is risky.","fact_ids":["sec17-R12","sec17-F10"]},{"text":"So are radio scanning and climate changes.","fact_ids":["sec17-R12","sec17-F10"]},{"text":"Internet and email add more risk.","fact_ids":["sec17-R12","sec17-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Under the heading turning dials can turn your head, the guide warns that working in-vehicle controls pulls your attention from the road. Entering a destination, scanning radio stations or changing climate settings can lead to a crash or a near-crash, and Internet and email access add even more risk. Each of these tasks takes your eyes to a screen or dial and your hand off the wheel. A few seconds of looking down at highway speed means covering a long distance without watching the road, which is exactly when hazards appear.","fact_ids":["sec17-R12","sec17-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":36,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s3","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Set up before you go","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13"]},"lines":[{"text":"Set climate, mirrors, radio, seat.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13"]},{"text":"Check email and voicemail first.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13"]},{"text":"Use a phone auto-reply.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13"]}],"narration":{"text":"Set the climate controls, mirrors, radio and seat before you start to drive. Check email, voicemail and other devices before you leave or after you arrive, not on the way. You can also set an auto-reply on your phone saying you are driving and will call back later, so you do not feel pressure to answer. These simple steps take a minute in the driveway and remove many of the reasons drivers reach for controls or devices while moving. Getting everything ready first lets you give the road your full attention. You can set an auto-reply on your phone saying you are driving and will call back later.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":43,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s4","kind":"concept","title":{"text":"Adjusting during a trip","fact_ids":["sec17-F14","sec17-F10"]},"lines":[{"text":"Use normal stops.","fact_ids":["sec17-F14","sec17-F10"]},{"text":"Or ask a passenger.","fact_ids":["sec17-F14","sec17-F10"]},{"text":"Radio, climate, navigation.","fact_ids":["sec17-F14","sec17-F10"]}],"narration":{"text":"Sometimes a control needs changing after you have started. The guide's answer is to use normal stops to adjust controls, or ask a passenger to adjust the radio, the climate settings or the navigation for you. A passenger can enter a new destination or change the temperature without anyone taking their eyes off the road. If you are driving alone, wait for a normal stop rather than doing it on the move. The goal is that the driver's eyes and hands stay on driving while the car is moving. Entering a destination, scanning radio stations or changing climate settings can lead to a crash or near-crash, and Internet and email access add more risk.","fact_ids":["sec17-F14","sec17-F10"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":46,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s5","kind":"trap","title":{"text":"Looking is a distraction","fact_ids":["sec17-F15","sec17-R07","sec17-F02"]},"lines":[{"text":"Crash scenes and police stops.","fact_ids":["sec17-F15","sec17-R07","sec17-F02"]},{"text":"Scenic views and billboards.","fact_ids":["sec17-F15","sec17-R07","sec17-F02"]},{"text":"Addresses and construction.","fact_ids":["sec17-F15","sec17-R07","sec17-F02"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is the trap. Many drivers think distraction only means doing something with their hands. Looking can be a distraction too. Staring at a crash scene, a vehicle stopped by police, a scenic view, a billboard, street addresses or construction work while driving is a distraction. Stay focused on driving and remain alert so you reach your destination safely, instead of studying the scenery you pass. Slowing down to stare at a crash, often called rubbernecking, can cause another crash behind the first one. A distraction is anything that keeps you from operating the car safely, and every distraction puts drivers, passengers and bystanders at risk.","fact_ids":["sec17-F15","sec17-R07","sec17-F02"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":42,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s6","kind":"self_check","title":{"text":"Check the setup rule","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14","sec17-F12"]},"lines":[{"text":"Mirrors, seat, radio, climate.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14","sec17-F12"]},{"text":"When do you set them?","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14","sec17-F12"]}],"narration":{"text":"Here is a quick check: when should you set your mirrors, your seat, the radio and the climate controls? Work it out before reading on. Set them before you start to drive. If something needs to change during the trip, use a normal stop to adjust it, or ask a passenger to adjust the radio, climate or navigation for you. Check your email and voicemail before you leave or after you arrive, not on the way, and consider an auto-reply on your phone saying you are driving and will call back later. Check email, voicemail and other devices before you leave or after you arrive, not on the way.","fact_ids":["sec17-F11","sec17-F14","sec17-F12"]},"estimated_narration_seconds":44,"media_role":"none","media_absence_reason":"text_first_pilot"},{"slide_id":"sec17-u03-s7","kind":"close","title":{"text":"Controls recap","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13","sec17-F14","sec17-F15","sec17-R07"]},"lines":[{"text":"Set up first; adjust at stops.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13","sec17-F14","sec17-F15","sec17-R07"]},{"text":"Do not stare at scenes.","fact_ids":["sec17-F10","sec17-F11","sec17-F12","sec17-F13","sec17-F14","sec17-F15","sec17-R07"]}],"narration":{"text":"Let us sum up. Working in-vehicle controls pulls your attention from the road: entering destinations, scanning radio stations and changing climate settings can lead to crashes or near-crashes, and Internet and email access add more risk.
